extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and parties litigating inter partes proceedings before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive rules and best practices for taking, noticing, conducting, and responding to discovery depositions (oral and written) in inter partes proceedings before the Board, including Fed. R. Civ. P. and 37 CFR §2.124 requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer before whom deposition is taken
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery depositions in Board inter partes proceedings may be taken before the persons designated by Fed. R. Civ. P. 28.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the United States, a Board proceeding discovery deposition “shall be taken before an officer authorized to administer oaths by the laws of the United States or of the place where the deposition is held, or before a person appointed by the court in which the action is pending.” In foreign countries, depositions may be taken pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 28(b) (e.g., before a U.S. consular official or anyone authorized by the foreign law). Some countries may forbid or limit taking testimony for use abroad; consult local counsel or the Office of Citizens Consular Services, Department of State, to determine permissibility and required procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirements for oral depositions (Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party who wants to depose a person by oral questions must give reasonable written notice to every other party stating time and place and, if known, the deponent’s name and address (or a general description sufficient to identify the person or class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether notice is reasonable depends on the circumstances. The closing of a party’s discovery period does not justify failing to provide reasonable notice. It is strongly recommended the deposing party contact the person sought to be deposed in advance to arrange a mutually convenient time. For additional procedural items see Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and filing for depositions on written questions (37 CFR §2.124)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party desiring to take a discovery deposition upon written questions shall serve notice upon each adverse party and shall file a copy of the notice, but not copies of the questions, with the Board; the notice shall state the name and address (if known) of the person whose deposition is to be taken and must be accompanied by the name or descriptive title of the officer before whom the deposition is to be taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the name is not known, the notice must provide a general description sufficient to identify the person or the class/group. Copies of the notice served on adverse parties must be accompanied by the written questions to be propounded on behalf of the deposing party. See 37 CFR §2.124(b)(2), (c), and (d)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Producing documents at deposition (Rule 34)
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice to a party deponent may be accompanied by a request under Rule 34 to produce documents and tangible things at the deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceeding under Rule 34 is appropriate when documents are few, simple, and closely related to oral examination. In requesting documents, the deposing party must allow at least 30 days between the request and the deposition (35 days if served by first-class mail, Express Mail, or overnight courier) to comply with Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(2)(A). For combining notice with a Rule 34 request see TBMP §406.01. A deposition must be taken prior to the expiration of the discovery period unless the parties stipulate otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming an organization as deponent (Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: In a notice or subpoena a party may name as the deponent an organization and must describe with reasonable particularity the matters for examination; the named organization must designate one or more officers, directors, or managing agents (or other persons) who consent to testify on its behalf and may set out the matters on which each person will testify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subpoena must advise a nonparty organization of its duty to designate. Each designated person must testify about information known or reasonably available to the organization. The paragraph does not preclude depositions by any other rule-authorized procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 30(b)(1) and 30(b)(6) depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposition of a party’s officer, director or managing agent in his/her individual capacity under Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(1) probes that individual's personal knowledge; a Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(6) deposition addresses the organization through its designated representative(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A witness may be deposed both in individual capacity under Rule 30(b)(1) and as a Rule 30(b)(6) designee. Prior individual testimony on a topic does not relieve the organization of its responsibility to designate a 30(b)(6) witness on that topic because individual testimony is not binding on the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to prepare 30(b)(6) designees
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization served with a Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(6) notice must prepare persons so they can give complete, knowledgeable, and binding answers as to matters known or reasonably available to the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The organization may produce multiple deponents or a single witness who reviews records to become familiar with the topics. If a designee is deficient, the organization must provide a substitute and prepare that person for areas where earlier representatives were uninformed. The production of an unprepared witness is tantamount to a failure to appear and can lead to motions to compel and sanctions; failure to designate or to appear may subject a party to motion or sanction under 37 CFR §2.120(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for failure to designate or unprepared 30(b)(6) witness
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may be subject to a motion to compel for failure to designate a person pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(6) or if such designated person fails to appear or fails to answer any question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions may be imposed for failure to attend or to provide a prepared witness. A second deposition and payment of costs may be required if the designee was unprepared. See cited case law (e.g., United Technologies; Tulip Computers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposition timing during discovery period
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery depositions must be taken, and noticed and taken, on or before the closing date of the discovery period as originally set or as reset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is recommended to initiate depositions early in the discovery period. The Board has discretion to schedule and may permit suspension of other discovery activities; depositions outside the period require stipulation or Board order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits and duration of depositions (Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(d)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless otherwise stipulated or ordered, a deposition is limited to 1 day of 7 hours; only actual deposition time counts against the limit (reasonable lunch and other breaks do not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For 30(b)(6) depositions, the deposition of each designated person is considered a separate deposition for the durational limit. Parties seeking additional time must show good cause consistent with Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(2). Additional time must be allowed if needed to fairly examine the deponent or if examination is impeded or delayed (e.g., power outage, health emergency). Orders directing shorter depositions or limited periods on several days are permitted. Parties expected to make reasonable accommodations to avoid motion practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote depositions (Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: On stipulation of the parties, or on motion granted by the Board, a deposition may be taken or attended by telephone or other remote means (e.g., video conferencing); for rule purposes the deposition takes place where the deponent answers questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A discovery deposition taken by remote means must be transcribed if submitted as evidence at trial. Current federal practice favors use of technological benefits; leave to take telephonic depositions should be liberally granted in appropriate cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-deposing a witness requires leave
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person has already been deposed in the case, a party must seek leave of the Board to take a second deposition if the parties have not stipulated thereto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board’s decision is guided by Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(2): consider whether discovery sought is unreasonably cumulative or duplicative, obtainable from other sources more convenient/less burdensome/less expensive, whether the seeking party had ample opportunity to obtain information, and whether burden/expense outweighs likely benefit. The requirement to seek leave does not apply to temporary recesses to complete deposition or gather additional materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for depositions on written questions (timelines and exchanges)
rubrics_metrics.description: For depositions on written questions, the notice must be served and copies filed; the deposing party must include written questions, and adverse parties may serve cross questions within 20 days (25 days if mailed), redirect within 10 days, and recross within 10 days (with adjusted times if mailed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written objections to questions may be served; substitute questions to respond to objections may be served within 10 days (15 days if mailed). The Board may extend these time periods for good cause. Within 10 days after the last date for questions/objections/substitutes, the deposing party mails the notice and all questions to the designated officer and serves copies on all adverse parties; the officer records each answer immediately after the corresponding question and then certifies and mails the transcript and exhibits to the deposing party. See 37 CFR §2.124(d)(1),(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections to questions and answers in depositions on written questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Written objections to questions may be served on a propounding party and must be served on every other adverse party; objections to questions and answers in depositions upon written questions may be considered at final hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If objections have been overcome by revised questions, the objecting party should file and serve notice of which objections no longer need be considered. Objections not maintained in a brief at final hearing may be considered waived by the Board. See TBMP §703.02(k) and TBMP §707.03(c), §707.04; 37 CFR §2.124(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form, signature, and certification of deposition on written questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The officer designated in the notice shall take the testimony of the witness in response to the questions and shall record each answer immediately after the corresponding question; the officer shall then certify the transcript and mail the transcript and exhibits to the party who took the deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For information concerning the form of a deposition taken in an inter partes proceeding, see 37 CFR §2.123(g) and TBMP §703.01(i). For signature issues see 37 CFR §2.123(e)(5) and TBMP §703.01(j). Certification and mailing occur within the timeline specified in 37 CFR §2.124(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation counting rules for multiple-deponent 30(b)(6) notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Even though more than one person may be designated to testify under a Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(6) notice, for purposes of the ten deposition limit under Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(a)(2)(A)(i), the 30(b)(6) deposition is treated as a single deposition; for the time limitation under Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(d)(1) the deposition of each designated person is considered a separate deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must account for both the numerical deposition limit and the per-deponent time limits when noticing or defending multi-person 30(b)(6) depositions. Advisory Committee notes and case law illustrate occasional adjustments and disputes.
